overview.title: 📖 Overview: Ending Chapter One, Opening Chapter Two
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין נֶעֱרָכִין פָּחוֹת מִסֶּלַע, וְלֹא יָתֵר עַל חֲמִשִּׁים סֶלַע
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the Gemara's discussion of one led to execution, resolving how an injured party's damages claim can reach his heirs — only where a court had already rendered judgment before his death, so the Torah's debt is then treated like a written loan. A mishna then rules on a pregnant woman condemned to death, executed at once unless she has already gone into labor, and the Gemara adds Shmuel's directive to strike her womb so the fetus dies first, alongside the law permitting one to cut open the abdomen of a woman who died in labor on Shabbat to try to save her child. The mishna's further ruling — that one may benefit from an executed woman's hair but not a slain animal's — is explained by the different moment each is rendered forbidden. The daf then closes the first chapter (הדרן עלך הכל מעריכין) and opens the second with a new mishna: a vow of valuation is never less than a sela nor more than fifty, with a dispute over what a poor man with limited funds actually owes.

slides.title: ⚖️ Collecting Damages From a Condemned Man's Heirs
slides.subtitle: Continuing yesterday's dispute between the tanna kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar

nodes.content: ❓ If one led to execution injured another, can the victim collect from his heirs after the execution?

columns.label: Rav Yosef
columns.content: The dispute is whether an ORAL loan is collectible from heirs at all

columns.label: Rabba
columns.content: Rather, everyone agrees an oral loan is NOT collectible — the dispute is whether a Torah-imposed debt (like damages) counts as a WRITTEN loan

nodes.content: 📜 Objection: a baraita rules that if a pit-digger dies from an ox's fall, his heirs must pay the ox's owner — proof that Torah-debts ARE collected from heirs!
✅ Resolved: that baraita describes a case where judges already sat and found him liable BEFORE he died — once a court renders judgment, the debt becomes like a written loan

slides.title: 🤰 Mishna: A Pregnant Woman Sentenced to Execution
slides.subtitle: Timing determines everything
rows: The fetus is considered part of her own body
Already sitting on the birthstool (labor begun)
Execution delayed until she gives birth
Once the fetus 'uproots' from its place, it is an independent body
His sin/guilt offering already slaughtered before execution
The blood is still sprinkled for him
A brief further delay is tolerable
New sin obligation arises at the moment of execution
Execution is NOT delayed to offer it
The court may not further afflict him by prolonging judgment

slides.title: 💔 Which Dies First — the Mother or the Fetus?
slides.subtitle: Shmuel's precaution, and a Shabbat exception to try to save a newborn

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Strike the pregnant woman opposite her womb before executing her, so the fetus dies first — sparing her the public disgrace of going into labor as she dies.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But we hold that in NATURAL death the fetus dies first anyway — proven from the law that a day-old infant can inherit his mother. Why the extra step?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: That principle applies only to natural death, where the fetus's weak vitality lets it be 'cut' first. In EXECUTION, the mother dies first — hence Shmuel's precaution.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman/Shmuel
lines.text: Separately: if a woman in labor dies on Shabbat, cut open her abdomen and remove the fetus — even desecrating Shabbat on the mere chance he is alive, though he never had a prior presumption of life at all.

slides.title: 💇 Hair of an Executed Woman vs. Hair of a Slain Animal
slides.subtitle: Same mishna, opposite rulings — why?

boxes.title: A Woman's Hair
items: Permitted to derive benefit from it after her execution
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: her DEATH is what forbids her — hair, unaffected by that moment, stays permitted
Alternate view (Rav): only a wig she designated for her daughter is permitted; her natural hair itself is not

boxes.title: An Animal's Hair
items: Forbidden to derive any benefit from it
The court's VERDICT itself renders the animal forbidden, even before it is killed
So the hair attached at the moment of the verdict is forbidden along with the rest

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: The Floor and Ceiling of a Valuation Vow
slides.subtitle: Chapter one closes, chapter two opens

steps.content: 1️⃣ No valuation is less than a sela — from 'your valuation shall be according to the shekel of the Sanctuary' — nor more than fifty sela, the Torah's maximum, fixed for a man aged 20–60
2️⃣ A poor man with only 5 sela vows his own erech, which the Torah fixes far higher: Rabbi Meir says he pays just 1 sela; the Rabbis say he must pay all 5
3️⃣ Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the verse gives only 'fifty' OR 'a shekel,' no in-between; the Rabbis read 'according to the means of the vower' as requiring payment of whatever he can actually afford

4️⃣ Rav Adda bar Ahava's case: a man with 5 sela vows his erech twice; paying the SECOND vow with 4 sela and the FIRST with the remaining 1 fulfills both — 'a later creditor who collects first keeps what he collected'

summary.principle: The chapter closes by drawing precise lines around a condemned person's residual legal status — his heirs' liability, the timing of a pregnant woman's execution, and what may still be used from her body — before the new chapter opens with equally precise floors and ceilings on the sums a valuation vow can actually demand.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Damages from a condemned man's estate are collectible only once a court judgment preceded his death
🤰 Pregnant woman: executed immediately unless labor began; fetus struck first to spare her disgrace; abdomen may be opened even on Shabbat to try to save it

columns.content: 💇 Her hair stays permitted (her death forbids her); an executed animal's hair does not (the verdict already forbids it)
💰 New mishna: valuation vows run from 1 sela to 50 sela, with a live dispute over a poor man's actual obligation

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: halakhic status turns on the exact moment a change takes effect — a judgment rendered, a fetus's independence, a verdict issued, or a fixed textual minimum and maximum

quiz.q: According to Rabba's resolution, why can the injured party in the pit-digger baraita collect from the heirs of the man who died?
o: Because he had already stood trial and been found liable before he died, so the debt is treated like a written loan
Because oral loans are always collectible from heirs
Because heirs are automatically liable for any debt their relative owed
Because the case involved a government decree
quiz.e: Rabba explains that once a court renders judgment before the debtor's death, the Torah-imposed debt is considered equivalent to a written loan and can be collected from his heirs.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what distinguishes a pregnant woman sentenced to execution who has not yet gone into labor from one who has already sat on the birthstool?
o: There is no difference — both are executed immediately
The first is executed immediately, since the fetus is part of her body; the second's execution is delayed until she gives birth, since the fetus has become an independent body
Both executions are delayed until birth
Only the second woman may appeal her sentence
quiz.e: The mishna rules that labor already begun makes the fetus an independent entity ('once it uproots'), which is why her execution is delayed, unlike the earlier case.

quiz.q: Why, according to Shmuel, does the court strike a pregnant woman opposite her womb before executing her?
o: To make the execution proceed more quickly
So that the fetus dies before her, sparing her the public disgrace of going into labor as she dies
As an additional form of punishment for her crime
So the fetus's body can be preserved for study
quiz.e: Shmuel's stated reason is 'so that she not come to disgrace' — the fetus is made to die first so she does not visibly go into labor during her execution.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, why may one derive benefit from an executed woman's hair, but not from the hide or hair of a court-condemned animal?
o: Her death is what renders her forbidden, so hair unaffected by that moment stays permitted; the animal is rendered forbidden by the court's VERDICT, before it is even killed, so its hair is included
Animals have no hair worth using
A woman's hair carries inherent sanctity
There is no genuine halakhic distinction between the two cases
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's distinction is about timing: the animal becomes forbidden at the moment of the verdict (before death), while the woman becomes forbidden only at the moment of her actual death — her hair is unaffected by that transition.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what are the minimum and maximum amounts one may be obligated to pay for a valuation (erech)?
o: No minimum, but a maximum of fifty sela
A minimum of one sela, with no maximum
A minimum of one sela (from 'according to the shekel of the Sanctuary') and a maximum of fifty sela, the Torah's highest fixed valuation
A minimum of five sela and a maximum of one hundred sela
quiz.e: The mishna and Gemara derive the floor of one sela from Leviticus 27:25 and the ceiling of fifty sela from the highest fixed valuation in Leviticus 27:3, for a man aged twenty to sixty.
